key_facts: **Keratolysis exfoliativa** is recurrent, painless superficial peeling of the palms (and soles), worse in warm weather.
Air-filled blisters burst into expanding **collarettes** of scale with no inflammation.
Benign, not contagious, not an allergy; often confused with hand eczema or tinea.
Irritant avoidance, emollients and keratolytic creams (urea, lactic acid); topical steroids do not help.
Scrape for fungus if one-sided or with a raised edge.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: A common, **benign, non-inflammatory** disorder of recurrent superficial peeling of the **palms** (soles less often), mostly in young active adults. Synonyms: exfoliative keratolysis, **dyshidrosis lamellosa sicca**, (recurrent) focal palmar peeling, lamellar dyshidrosis. Often under-recognised and mislabelled as "hand eczema", which is why patients arrive having failed topical steroids.

sub: Young adults; often associated with sweaty hands; summer flares.

ul: Cause unknown; may run in families.

Splitting occurs **within the stratum corneum** — corneodesmosomes (the "rivets" between corneocytes) appear to break down prematurely, so sheets of horny layer detach (Chang et al., BJD 2012 described it as a distinct peeling entity; no causative gene identified).
**Aggravating factors:** heat/summer, **palmar hyperhidrosis**, and irritants — water, soap, detergents, solvents, friction. Roughly half of patients notice summer worsening.
Not an allergy, not infective, and not steroid-responsive inflammation.
Unknown; possibly a variant of mild pompholyx or an inherited keratin defect; friction, water and detergents aggravate.
**"It's eczema, use steroid"**: there is no inflammation, so steroids are wasted and thin the skin.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: The outer **stratum corneum splits**, forming air-filled blisters that peel.

mech.t: Cohesion within the stratum corneum fails, creating an air space.
mech.caption: A split within the stratum corneum forms an air-filled blister.

mech.t: The roof peels outwards, leaving rings of scale over normal skin.
mech.caption: Air blister → collarette → peeling.

mech.t: New stratum corneum forms beneath within 1–3 weeks.

histo: Rarely needed: splitting within the upper stratum corneum without inflammation.

head: Feature
Detail
rows: One or more tiny **air-filled** (not fluid-filled) superficial blisters on palms/fingers
Blisters burst → **expanding collarettes of scale** → round/oval peeled patches; multiple lamellae may peel
**Not itchy**; peeled areas can feel tender/dry and crack
Absent or minimal (no oedema, no vesicles with fluid, no lichenification)
Split can be deeper — skin feels **hard and numb** before it sheds (explains the numbness patients describe)
Heals to normal skin, then **recurs every few weeks**; chronic over years; often worse in summer

ul: **Clinical** — history of recurrent non-itchy peeling + collarettes on non-inflamed palms.
Supportive tests if doubt: **skin scrapings negative** for fungus; **patch tests negative**; biopsy (rarely needed) shows cleavage within the stratum corneum.

**Pearl — the numbness:** usually explained by thick, deeply split fingertip horny layer; still ask about diabetes, B12/alcohol, carpal tunnel symptoms and vibration-tool use if numbness is persistent, sensory-distributed or present when skin is intact (diabetic neuropathy is a sensible safety-net).

sections.title: Management
blocks: **Explain first:** benign, cosmetic-nuisance condition, recurrent, not contagious and not an allergy; tends to improve with age; steroids won't help (stop them — avoids palmar atrophy and wasted courses).

ul: **Irritant avoidance:** cotton-lined waterproof gloves for wet work; soap substitutes; dry hands thoroughly.

**Emollient / keratolytic hand creams**, applied frequently: **urea** (e.g. 5–10% for maintenance, 10–25% for peeling — several UK OTC brands), **lactic acid** or **salicylic acid**-containing products; silicone/dimeticone barrier creams. US sources cite higher strengths (urea 20–40%, ammonium lactate 12%, salicylic acid 6%) — UK availability is limited, so use licensed UK products/specials per formulary.
**Treat hyperhidrosis** if present (topical aluminium chloride hexahydrate at night; refer for tap-water iontophoresis if severe) — reduces summer flares.

blocks: **Specialist options (refer if severe, painful fissuring, or diagnostic doubt):** acitretin (teratogenic, specialist-only, Pregnancy Prevention Programme), hand **PUVA**/photochemotherapy — limited evidence, reserved for refractory cases given skin-cancer and burden trade-offs.

ladder.t: Stop steroids: they don’t help and risk atrophy. Cotton-lined gloves for wet work; soap substitutes; dry hands well.
**Urea** 5–10% maintenance, 10–25% for peeling; lactic or salicylic acid creams; dimeticone barrier creams. Use licensed UK products per formulary.
Aluminium chloride hexahydrate at night; iontophoresis if severe.
Acitretin (teratogenic, specialist only) or hand PUVA for refractory cases: limited evidence.

refer.t: Peeling fingertips in a **child with fever ≥ 5 days**: think Kawasaki disease.
Painful fissuring, severe disease or diagnostic doubt: dermatology.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Peeling fingertips in a **child with fever** for 5 days or more: think Kawasaki disease (urgent).
Peeling after a sore throat and rash: scarlet fever.
Tender fissures and secondary irritant dermatitis.

pearls: "Peeling but not itchy, not red, worse in summer, steroid-proof" = think KE before re-issuing steroid.
Scrape any one-handed or treatment-resistant peeling to exclude tinea before labelling KE.
Avoid picking/peeling the lamellae — trim loose edges with clean scissors to reduce painful cracks.
Fingertip numbness that persists between episodes → examine/assess for neuropathy.

quiz.a: No: tiny air-filled blisters that burst into collarettes.
KE isn’t inflammatory; steroids don’t help and risk palmar atrophy.
Urea (5–10% maintenance, 10–25% for peeling) or lactic / salicylic acid creams.
